long-run-costs-s1.title: Lindqvist Kayaks: plant size and long-run cost

table.caption: The lowest total cost of each yearly output when the firm can choose any plant size (invented data for practice)

long-run-costs-s2.title: A firm's long-run average total cost curve

long-run-costs-s3.title: Sunmere Solar grows its factory
long-run-costs-s3.text: Sunmere Solar doubles every input it uses: workers, assembly lines, floor space and machines. Its weekly output of solar panels rises from 1,000 to 2,500. Years later, at a much larger size, it doubles every input again, and weekly output rises from 4,000 to 7,000. Input prices stay the same throughout. (An invented business, for practice.)

items.q: Use the table. What is long-run average total cost at 500 kayaks a year, in dollars?

why.correct: LRATC is long-run total cost divided by output: $3{,}500 \div 500 = 7$ dollars a kayak.

mistakes.why: That is the extra cost of the last 100 kayaks per kayak (1,100 / 100). LRATC divides the long-run total cost by output.
That is long-run total cost. Divide it by the 500 kayaks.

items.q: Use the table. Over which range of output does the firm have economies of scale?
options: From 300 to 400 kayaks, where LRATC stays at \$6
From 400 to 600 kayaks, where long-run total cost rises fastest
From 100 to 300 kayaks, where LRATC falls from \$10 to \$6
From 100 to 600 kayaks, because long-run total cost rises

why.correct: LRATC is 10, 8, 6, 6, 7 and 8 dollars. It falls from 100 to 300 kayaks (economies of scale), is flat from 300 to 400 and rises after 400.
options: LRATC is flat there: constant returns to scale.
LRATC rises from 6 to 8 there: diseconomies of scale.
Right: LRATC is 10, 8, then 6.
Total cost always grows with output; scale is judged by the average, which falls and later rises.

items.q: Use the table. What is the firm's minimum efficient scale?
options: 300 kayaks a year
400 kayaks a year
100 kayaks a year
600 kayaks a year

why.correct: Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output at which long-run average total cost is lowest: 300 kayaks, at \$6.
options: Right: the smallest output at which LRATC reaches its lowest value, \$6.
LRATC is also \$6 at 400, but 300 is the smallest output at that lowest level.
At 100 kayaks LRATC is \$10, its highest value.
At 600 kayaks LRATC has risen to \$8: diseconomies of scale.

items.q: Use the table. Buyers in the whole market want about 30,000 kayaks a year at a price near \$6. About how many firms like this one can produce at the lowest long-run average total cost?
options: About 5 firms, each making 6,000 kayaks
One firm, because one large firm has the lowest cost
About 300 firms, each making 100 kayaks
About 75 to 100 firms, each making 300 to 400 kayaks

why.correct: Minimum efficient scale is small (300 kayaks) next to the market (30,000), so many firms can each produce at the lowest average cost. A small minimum efficient scale relative to demand supports a market with many firms.
options: A firm making 6,000 kayaks would be far into diseconomies of scale, with high average cost.
LRATC rises past 400 kayaks, so one huge firm would have a higher average cost.
At 100 kayaks LRATC is \$10, well above the lowest level.
Right: 30,000 / 400 = 75 and 30,000 / 300 = 100, so the market can hold many low-cost firms.

items.q: In the graph, LRATC slopes downward at small outputs. Which is a likely reason?
options: A fixed input is shared by more workers
Larger firms buy materials in bulk at a discount
Managers find it harder to coordinate a larger firm
Buyers pay more for the product of a larger firm

why.correct: On the falling part of LRATC the firm has economies of scale: specialized machines and workers and bulk discounts lower cost per unit as the firm grows.
options: That is diminishing marginal returns, a short-run idea; in the long run no input is fixed.
Right: bulk buying is a source of economies of scale.
That raises average cost: a source of diseconomies of scale.
LRATC is a cost curve; buyers' prices do not shape it.

items.q: In the graph, what does the part of LRATC to the right of its lowest point show?
options: Economies of scale: average cost falls as the firm grows
Diseconomies of scale
Diminishing marginal returns from a fixed plant
Minimum efficient scale, the lowest average cost

why.correct: Past its lowest point, LRATC rises: a larger firm has a higher cost per unit, often from the strain of coordinating many workers and sites.
options: Economies of scale are on the falling part, to the left.
Right: LRATC rising with output is diseconomies of scale.
That is a short-run idea; LRATC lets every input change.
Minimum efficient scale is at the bottom of the curve, not to its right.

items.q: In the graph, a firm is producing on the downward-sloping part of LRATC. If it builds a larger plant and produces more, its long-run average total cost will
options: rise, because a larger plant costs more in total
stay the same, because each input grew by the same share
rise, because diminishing marginal returns set in
fall, as it moves down the curve

why.correct: Left of minimum efficient scale, growing lowers long-run average total cost. That is the cost advantage of size in industries with large economies of scale.
options: Total cost rises, but it is spread over even more units, so the average falls here.
Equal growth in inputs can still lower cost per unit when there are economies of scale.
Diminishing returns need a fixed input; in the long run none is fixed.
Right: on the falling part, more output means a lower average cost.

items.q: In the scenario, the first doubling of inputs shows
options: increasing returns to scale, because output more than doubles
decreasing returns to scale, because output rises by less than inputs
constant returns to scale, because each input doubled
diminishing marginal returns, because one input is fixed

why.correct: Returns to scale compare output growth with input growth when every input changes. Output going from 1,000 to 2,500 (2.5 times) when inputs double is increasing returns to scale.
options: Right: output rises 2.5 times when every input doubles.
Output rose by more than double (1,000 to 2,500), not less.
Constant returns would mean output exactly doubles, to 2,000.
No input is fixed here; every input doubled.

items.q: In the scenario, input prices do not change. What happens to the firm's long-run average total cost after the first doubling?
options: It rises: the firm has diseconomies of scale
It stays the same: total cost doubled
It falls: the firm has economies of scale
It falls: the firm has diminishing marginal returns

why.correct: With input prices fixed, doubling every input doubles total cost. Output rises 2.5 times, so cost per unit falls to $\frac{2}{2.5} = 0.8$ of what it was: economies of scale.
options: Cost per panel rises only if output grows by less than the inputs.
Total cost doubled, but output more than doubled, so the average fell.
Right: costs double but output rises 2.5 times, so cost per panel falls.
Diminishing marginal returns would raise costs, and they need a fixed input.

items.q: In the scenario, the second doubling raises output from 4,000 to 7,000 panels. Which describes the firm at this larger size?
options: Increasing returns to scale and economies of scale
Constant returns to scale and minimum efficient scale
Decreasing returns to scale and diseconomies of scale
Diminishing marginal returns from its fixed factory

why.correct: Inputs (and total cost) double, but output grows only 1.75 times, so cost per panel rises: decreasing returns to scale bring diseconomies of scale.
options: Output rises 1.75 times, less than the doubling of inputs.
Constant returns would need output to reach exactly 8,000.
Right: output grows by less than double, so cost per panel rises.
The factory doubled too: no input is fixed.

items.q: What is the long-run average total cost curve?
options: The lowest average cost of each output, any plant size
The average cost of each output with the plant held fixed
The extra cost of one more unit with a fixed plant
The total cost of the largest plant the firm could build

why.correct: In the long run every input can change, so for each output the firm chooses the plant size with the lowest cost. LRATC traces those lowest average costs.
options: Right: LRATC lets the firm pick the best plant size for each output.
That is a short-run ATC curve.
That is short-run marginal cost.
LRATC is an average for each output, not one plant's total.

items.q: Label the axes and the curve of a firm's long-run cost graph.

why.correct: Cost goes on the vertical axis and quantity of output on the horizontal axis; the U-shaped curve is LRATC, long-run average total cost.

items.q: Mark the firm's minimum efficient scale on its long-run average total cost curve.

why.correct: Minimum efficient scale is where LRATC first reaches its lowest level: the bottom of the curve.

items.q: How do diminishing marginal returns differ from diseconomies of scale?
options: They are two names for the same rise in cost
Diminishing returns happen in the long run; diseconomies in the short run
Diseconomies of scale come from rising input prices
One needs a fixed input; the other needs growth in each input

why.correct: Diminishing marginal returns: in the short run, more of one input added to a fixed input. Diseconomies of scale: in the long run, all inputs grow and cost per unit rises, often from coordination problems.
options: Both raise costs, but they have different causes and time frames.
It is the other way round.
Diseconomies come from the strain of size, with input prices unchanged.
Right: one is a short-run idea, the other a long-run idea.

items.q: In the long run, a bakery chain can make 1,500 loaves a day at a lowest total cost of \$9,000. What is its long-run average total cost per loaf, in dollars?

why.correct: LRATC = long-run total cost divided by output = $9{,}000 \div 1{,}500 = 6$ dollars a loaf.

mistakes.why: That divides output by cost. Average cost is cost divided by output: 9,000 / 1,500.
That is long-run total cost. Divide it by the 1,500 loaves.

items.q: Which of these are likely causes of diseconomies of scale? Select all that apply.
options: Messages pass through many layers of managers and get delayed
The firm spreads its design costs over more units
The firm gets a discount for buying steel in large amounts
The firm can afford a specialized machine that speeds up production

why.correct: Diseconomies of scale come from the problems of coordinating a very large organization; bulk discounts, specialized equipment and spreading costs over more units are economies of scale.
options: Yes: coordination gets harder as a firm grows.
No: spreading fixed costs over more output lowers cost per unit, an economy of scale.
No: bulk discounts lower cost per unit, an economy of scale.
No: specialized capital is an economy of scale.

items.q: In one industry, minimum efficient scale is half of the quantity the whole market buys. Which market is most likely?
options: A market with hundreds of small firms
A market with a few large firms
A market where firm size does not affect cost
A market where each firm makes one unit

why.correct: When minimum efficient scale is large compared with total demand, only a few firms can produce at the lowest cost, so the industry tends to have few, large firms.
options: Small firms would be far up the falling part of LRATC with high costs.
Right: at most two firms can each reach minimum efficient scale.
This industry has large economies of scale, so size matters a great deal.
Tiny firms would have far higher average costs.

items.q: A firm grows from very small to very large, with input prices unchanged. Put the stages of its LRATC in order.
options: Economies of scale: LRATC falls
Minimum efficient scale: LRATC first reaches its lowest level
Constant returns to scale: LRATC stays flat
Diseconomies of scale: LRATC rises

why.correct: Growth first lowers cost per unit, then cost per unit levels off at its lowest value starting at minimum efficient scale, and finally rises as size becomes hard to manage.
